posts.title: agent failures are logging failures
posts.hook: Most agent failures in production aren't model failures. They're "I have no idea what happened between step 3 and step 7" failures.
posts.body:
Most agent failures in production aren't model failures. They're "I have no idea what happened between step 3 and step 7" failures.

I run a multi-agent pipeline that does enrichment, scoring, and outbound sequencing. When it breaks, the model almost never hallucinated. What actually happened: a tool call returned an empty array, the next agent treated that as "no results" instead of "API timeout," and the whole chain confidently moved forward with garbage data.

The fix wasn't a better model. It was structured logging at every agent handoff.

Now every agent writes a status object before passing context downstream. Tool call result, token count, confidence flag, and a hash of the input it received vs. what the previous agent said it sent.

Three things that changed:

✅ Mean time to debug dropped from 45 minutes to under 5
✅ I catch silent failures same-day instead of finding them in a weekly pipeline audit
✅ I can actually replay a failed run from the exact point it diverged

The agent SDK conversation is exciting. But the boring work of making agents observable is what separates demo-grade from production-grade.

remixes.label: tactical-breakdown
remixes.hook: I spent 3 hours debugging an agent failure last week. The model was fine. The logs were useless.
remixes.body:
I spent 3 hours debugging an agent failure last week. The model was fine. The logs were useless.

Here's what I found: my enrichment agent called an API, got a 200 response with an empty payload, passed that downstream, and the scoring agent silently scored zero leads. No error. No warning. Just a quiet pipeline that looked healthy but produced nothing.

The fix wasn't better prompts or a smarter model. It was three things:

1. Typed contracts between agents. Every handoff validates the shape and count of what's being passed. Empty array from an enrichment step? That's an exception, not a valid result.

2. Agent-level trace IDs. Every agent stamps a correlation ID on its output. When something breaks, I grep one ID and get the full chain.

3. Canary assertions. Before the scoring agent runs, it checks: did I receive at least N records? If not, halt and surface why.

None of this is novel. It's the same observability discipline backend engineers have used for years. We just forgot to bring it into agent orchestration because the demos never show the failure modes.

The gap between "works in a notebook" and "works in production" is almost entirely logging, validation, and error taxonomy.
remixes.cta: What's breaking silently in your agent pipelines right now? Most people don't know until a customer notices.

remixes.label: contrarian-flip
remixes.hook: Hot take: prompt engineering matters way less than error engineering for production agents.
remixes.body:
Hot take: prompt engineering matters way less than error engineering for production agents.

Everyone's obsessing over system prompts, temperature settings, and chain-of-thought strategies. Meanwhile their agents fail silently in production because nobody defined what a failure even looks like.

I learned this running a GTM pipeline that enriches, scores, and sequences leads automatically. My biggest wins didn't come from better prompts. They came from building an error taxonomy.

Three categories changed everything:

Retriable failures: API timeouts, rate limits, temporary network blips. These get automatic retry with backoff.

Data failures: empty responses, malformed payloads, missing required fields. These halt the pipeline and alert me.

Logic failures: the model interpreted instructions differently than intended. These are the hardest to catch and require golden-path test cases.

Once I categorized errors this way, debugging went from "something broke, start guessing" to "check which category, apply the playbook."

The irony is that this is boring, well-established software engineering. But the agent ecosystem skipped straight to "autonomous AI" without building the foundation that makes autonomy safe.
remixes.cta: Do you have an error taxonomy for your agents, or is every failure a surprise?

posts.title: your ICP is a fossil
posts.hook: Your ICP definition is probably 18 months old and based on who bought last year, not who's buying now.
posts.body:
Your ICP definition is probably 18 months old and based on who bought last year, not who's buying now.

I audit GTM stacks for a living. The pattern is consistent: teams spend weeks A/B testing subject lines and email copy while targeting companies that no longer fit their product.

Markets shift. Budgets move. New categories emerge. The company that was a perfect fit in Q1 2025 might have frozen that budget line entirely.

What I do instead: pull closed-won from the last 90 days, enrich with current firmographic and technographic signals, then diff against the ICP doc. Every quarter.

Last time I ran this for a client, 3 of their 5 ICP criteria were still valid. Two were completely stale. They'd been burning outbound budget on companies that matched a profile from a market that doesn't exist anymore.

The enrichment run takes about 20 minutes with the right scripts. The ICP refresh conversation takes an hour. Compare that to the months of pipeline you waste targeting ghosts.

Subject line optimization gets you maybe 3-5% lift. Targeting the right companies gets you 40%+ lift on qualified pipeline.
posts.cta: When's the last time you actually diffed your ICP against recent closed-won data?

remixes.label: data-autopsy
remixes.hook: I pulled a client's closed-won data last month and compared it to their ICP doc. Less than 30% overlap.
remixes.body:
I pulled a client's closed-won data last month and compared it to their ICP doc. Less than 30% overlap.

Their ICP said: Series B SaaS, 50-200 employees, North America, VP Sales buyer.

Their actual closed-won from the last two quarters: bootstrapped companies with 15-40 people, often with a founder as the buyer, heavy in fintech and healthcare verticals they'd never targeted.

The market had moved. Their product had evolved. Their best customers looked nothing like the persona pinned to the sales team's Notion page.

Here's the process I now run quarterly:

1. Export closed-won from the last 90 days. Pull firmographics, tech stack, and the trigger that started the conversation.

2. Cluster the data. Look for patterns you didn't target intentionally. Those accidental wins are often your best signal.

3. Diff against the current ICP doc. Where do they diverge? That divergence is either a positioning problem or an ICP update waiting to happen.

4. Check your disqualified leads. How many of them actually match the new pattern better than the old ICP?

The ICP isn't a document you write once. It's a hypothesis you validate against every cohort of new customers. Treat it like code that needs regular commits, not a constitution carved in stone.
remixes.cta: Try this: pull your last 20 closed-won deals and see how many actually match your documented ICP. The number might surprise you.

remixes.label: contrarian-flip
remixes.hook: Controversial opinion: most ICP exercises are just confirmation bias with a spreadsheet.
remixes.body:
Controversial opinion: most ICP exercises are just confirmation bias with a spreadsheet.

You sit in a room. You describe your best customers. You reverse-engineer traits they share. You write it up in a doc. You hand it to sales and marketing. Everyone nods.

The problem: you just described who already bought, not who should buy next. And the market between then and now might look completely different.

Budgets shifted. New categories emerged. A competitor folded and their customers are looking. A regulation hit an industry and suddenly your product solves a compliance problem you never positioned for.

None of that shows up in a backward-looking ICP.

What actually works is treating your ICP like a living query, not a static document. Signals over segments. Instead of "Series B, 50-200 employees, North America," you define trigger conditions: just raised a round, posted a job for a role your product replaces, lost their incumbent vendor, published a blog about the exact problem you solve.

That's not an ICP. That's a detection model. And it updates itself because the signals are real-time, not historical.

The companies doing this well aren't spending weeks on persona workshops. They're building signal monitors that surface accounts when buying conditions are true, regardless of whether they fit the legacy profile.
remixes.cta: When's the last time a deal closed that didn't match your ICP at all? That outlier might be your next core segment.

posts.title: replaced SDR workflow not SDRs
posts.hook: I keep seeing "we replaced our SDR team with AI" posts. That framing misses what actually happened.
posts.body:
I keep seeing "we replaced our SDR team with AI" posts. That framing misses what actually happened.

You didn't replace people. You replaced a workflow that was always inefficient. Manual list building, manual enrichment, manual sequencing, manual CRM entry. That workflow was broken before AI. It just had humans absorbing the pain.

What a Claude + API + SQLite pipeline actually replaces:

🔧 The 4 hours/week an SDR spent copying data between Apollo and Salesforce
🔧 The enrichment step where someone manually googles a prospect to personalize line 1
🔧 The list building where someone filters the same boolean search for the 200th time

The part it doesn't replace: reading a reply, understanding context, having a real conversation, navigating a complex buying committee.

I built an outbound system last month that books qualified meetings. It handles enrichment, scoring, sequencing, and initial send. But every reply goes to a human. Every meeting is run by a human. Every deal is closed by a human.

The goal was never to eliminate SDRs. It was to stop asking $60k/year humans to do work that a $200/month API bill handles better.
posts.cta: Are you automating the workflow or actually trying to remove the human? Big difference in how the system performs long-term.

inspired_by.author: Saad Khan
inspired_by.summary: We replaced a 3-person SDR team with a Clay + Claude workflow and booked 40% more qualified meetings last month. Not because AI is magic — because we stopped sending generic sequences to unqualified accounts. The hard truth: most outbound problems are data problems, not copy problems. Here's the exact stack we use.

remixes.label: workflow-anatomy
remixes.hook: Here's everything an SDR does in a day that has nothing to do with selling.
remixes.body:
Here's everything an SDR does in a day that has nothing to do with selling.

Copy-paste a company name into LinkedIn. Find the right contact. Copy their email into a spreadsheet. Enrich it with a tool. Check if they're already in the CRM. If not, create a record. Write a first-touch email. Log the activity. Set a follow-up reminder. Repeat 80 times.

That's not selling. That's data entry with a quota.

When people say "AI replaced our SDR team," what they actually mean is: we automated the data pipeline that SDRs were manually operating. The list building, the enrichment, the CRM hygiene, the sequence enrollment.

A Claude Code script connected to Apollo, Exa, and a SQLite database does that work in minutes. Not because AI is smarter than an SDR, but because those tasks are deterministic. They have clear inputs, clear outputs, and clear rules. That's what automation is for.

What it doesn't replace: reading a prospect's recent LinkedIn post and connecting it to a real business problem. Navigating a multi-threaded deal. Picking up on tone in a discovery call. Building trust over multiple touchpoints.

The SDRs who are vulnerable aren't the ones who sell well. They're the ones whose entire day is the mechanical pipeline. The role doesn't disappear. The workflow does. And that's a different conversation entirely.
remixes.cta: Map out your SDR's actual daily tasks. How much is selling vs. data logistics? That ratio tells you what to automate.

remixes.label: reframe-narrative
remixes.hook: "We replaced our SDRs with AI" is the new "we moved to the cloud." It sounds impressive but says almost nothing.
remixes.body:
"We replaced our SDRs with AI" is the new "we moved to the cloud." It sounds impressive but says almost nothing.

What did you actually replace? Because when I dig into these stories, the answer is almost always the same: they automated the pre-selling workflow. Lead sourcing, enrichment, list building, CRM entry, sequence enrollment.

That work was always automatable. We just didn't have good enough tooling until now. The SDR wasn't adding judgment to those steps. They were absorbing the friction of bad tooling.

Here's what I think the real story is, and why the framing matters:

If you frame it as "replaced SDRs," you'll try to automate everything the SDR did, including the parts that need human judgment. And your pipeline quality will tank.

If you frame it as "replaced the workflow," you'll automate the mechanical parts and redeploy human effort to the high-leverage moments: personalized outreach, creative sequencing, deal strategy.

I've built both versions. The "replace everything" version gets impressive demo metrics and terrible conversion rates. The "replace the workflow" version is less flashy but actually closes deals.

The framing isn't semantics. It determines what you build, what you measure, and whether the system actually works six months later.

Every "replaced our SDRs" post should come with a follow-up showing pipeline quality and conversion metrics. Most won't, because those numbers tell a more complicated story.
remixes.cta: Have you seen a team that actually improved conversion rates after fully automating outbound? Genuinely curious, because the examples I've seen tell a different story.

posts.title: cursor 500M and the build-your-own wave
posts.hook: Cursor crossing $500M ARR tells you something bigger than "AI coding tools are hot."
posts.body:
Cursor crossing $500M ARR tells you something bigger than "AI coding tools are hot."

It tells you the number of people who can build software just mass-expanded. And that has second-order effects nobody's pricing in.

When building gets cheaper, the "build vs. buy" math flips for thousands of teams. The SaaS tool that costs $500/mo and sort of fits your workflow now competes against "I'll just build exactly what I need this weekend."

I've been living this. My entire GTM stack is built, not bought. Enrichment, scoring, CRM, outbound sequencing, analytics. Claude Code plus APIs plus a SQLite database. Total monthly cost is under $300 for what would be $3,000+ in point tools.

And I'm not a software engineer by training. I was a plumber for ten years. The coding agent is the gap closer.

This is the real disruption. Not AI replacing developers. AI enabling a new class of builder who thinks in systems but never had the syntax to express it. GTM operators, RevOps people, founders. People who know exactly what they need but couldn't code it until now.

Cursor's $500M is the leading indicator. The lagging indicator will be point-tool churn rates 18 months from now.
posts.cta: What's the first tool you'd replace with a custom build if coding cost dropped to near-zero for you?

inspired_by.summary: Cursor just crossed $500M ARR and they're not slowing down. The developer tools category is being completely rewritten in 18 months. What's underappreciated: this isn't IDE replacement — it's the first time a dev tool has become the actual reasoning layer for engineers. Every tool category above and below it gets repriced.

posts.title: cold outbound isn't dead it evolved
posts.hook: Open rates down 60%. Reply rates under 1%. Cold outbound is dead, right? No. Lazy outbound is dead.
posts.body:
Open rates down 60%. Reply rates under 1%. Cold outbound is dead, right?

No. Lazy outbound is dead.

The playbook that died: buy a list of 10,000 contacts, write 3 email variants, blast them through a sequence tool, pray for replies.

The playbook that works now: detect a signal, enrich the context around that signal, reach out with something specific to their situation, on the channel where they're actually active.

I monitor Reddit, job boards, and tech stack changes for intent signals. When a company posts about a problem my tool solves, that's not a cold lead. That's someone who publicly said they need help.

The sequence for those leads looks nothing like traditional cold outbound:

✅ Signal detected (Reddit post, job listing, G2 review)
✅ Company enriched with current stack, headcount, funding stage
✅ Personalized first line referencing the specific signal
✅ One email. Not a 7-touch sequence.

Reply rate on signal-based outreach last month: 14%. Compare that to the sub-1% everyone's complaining about.

The difference isn't copy. It's timing and relevance. You're reaching someone who has the problem right now, and you're proving you know that.

I analyzed 5,000 outbound emails from a client's campaign last quarter. 4,800 of them had no reason to exist.

The 200 emails that actually had a signal (job post, tech change, funding round, community question) generated 90% of the replies.

posts.title: agent orchestration context is the bottleneck
posts.hook: Ran a 6-agent pipeline last week. The model was fine. The context passing between agents was a disaster.
posts.body:
Ran a 6-agent pipeline last week. The model was fine. The context passing between agents was a disaster.

Agent 1 researches a company. Agent 2 enriches contacts. Agent 3 scores them. Agent 4 writes sequences. Agent 5 reviews. Agent 6 schedules.

Sounds clean on a whiteboard. In practice, by the time agent 4 starts writing, it's working with a compressed summary of what agents 1-3 found. Key details get lost. The personalization that agent 1 surfaced from a Reddit thread? Gone by agent 4.

The fix was embarrassingly simple. I stopped passing summaries and started passing structured objects. Each agent writes to a shared JSON schema. The next agent reads the specific fields it needs, not a prose summary of everything that happened.

Agent 4 doesn't need the full research output. It needs: company pain point (string), evidence source (url), contact role (string), and relevance score (float). That's it.

Pipeline quality jumped immediately. Not because the model got smarter. Because the model stopped losing information at every handoff.

The SDK and orchestration layer conversation is important. But the mundane work of designing your inter-agent data contract matters more than which framework you pick.

remixes.label: structured-handoff-blueprint
remixes.hook: Your AI agents aren't dumb. They're just playing telephone.
remixes.body:
Your AI agents aren't dumb. They're just playing telephone.

I watched a perfectly good Claude Opus agent write garbage outreach last week. Not because it can't write. Because by the time it received the research from three upstream agents, the context had been compressed into a lossy paragraph.

The company had a specific pain point buried in a 10-K filing. Agent 1 found it. Agent 2 summarized it as "financial challenges." Agent 3 passed that along. Agent 4 wrote a cold email about "financial challenges" that could apply to literally any company on earth.

The fix wasn't better models. It was better data contracts between agents.

I started defining typed objects at every handoff point. Company research returns a struct with fields: pain_signals (array), tech_stack (array), recent_events (array with dates), hiring_patterns (object). Not prose. Not summaries. Structured data that downstream agents can reference by field.

Context loss dropped by roughly 80%. The outreach went from generic to specific overnight. Same models, same prompts, different plumbing.

The bottleneck in multi-agent systems isn't intelligence. It's information architecture.

remixes.label: context-window-math
remixes.hook: I did the math on context loss in a 6-agent pipeline. By agent 4, you've lost about 60% of the original signal. That's not a model problem. That's an engineering problem.
remixes.body:
I did the math on context loss in a 6-agent pipeline. By agent 4, you've lost about 60% of the original signal. That's not a model problem. That's an engineering problem.

Here's what happens. Agent 1 researches a company and produces 2,000 tokens of useful detail. Agent 2 gets a 400-token summary because you're trying to stay under context limits. Agent 3 compresses further. By the time the writing agent starts drafting, it's working with the equivalent of a Wikipedia stub.

I tracked this across 50 companies in a real pipeline. Measured how many specific details from the original research survived to the final output. The number was brutal. Company-specific pain points, recent news, tech stack details. Most of it evaporated.

Two things actually helped. First, a shared memory layer that any agent can query directly instead of relying on what the previous agent chose to pass along. Second, separating the "what to pass" decision from the agents themselves. A routing layer decides what downstream agents need and pulls it from the shared store.

The agents got better at their jobs the moment I stopped asking them to also be good at summarizing for each other.

🔧 Build logs. "Here's what I built this week, here's what broke, here's what I learned." People follow the journey.

🔧 Problem breakdowns. Take a common pain point in your space, show the root cause most people miss, share your approach.

🔧 Contrarian takes backed by data. Not hot takes for engagement. Actual positions you hold based on what you've seen building.

The common thread: specificity. Tool names, numbers, screenshots, actual workflows. Generic advice gets scrolled past. Receipts get saved and shared.

Your LinkedIn isn't a billboard for your product. It's a live demo of how you think.

posts.title: three launches one win
posts.hook: I've shipped three major things this year. One flopped completely. One is breaking even. One is actually working. The pattern is obvious in hindsight.
posts.body:
I've shipped three major things this year. One flopped completely. One is breaking even. One is actually working. The pattern is obvious in hindsight.

The flop: I built something I thought was cool. Technically interesting. Solved a problem I personally had. Didn't validate that anyone else had it. Shipped it, posted about it, got polite "cool project" comments. Zero signups.

The break-even: I validated the problem existed but built the wrong interface. The backend pipeline was solid. The way users interacted with it was friction-heavy. People churned after the first week because the workflow required too many manual steps.

The one that works: I found the problem in public forums where people were actively complaining about it. Built the pipeline first, made the interface dead simple, and launched where those same people hang out.

The difference wasn't effort. I worked equally hard on all three. The difference was where I started.

Flop started with "I want to build this."
Break-even started with "people have this problem."
Win started with "people are publicly asking for help with this specific thing, right now."

Building is the easy part when you have a coding agent. Finding the right thing to build is still the whole game.

Built three things this year. The one that worked wasn't the most technically impressive. It was the one where I didn't come up with the idea.

Project 1: I saw a technical gap in the market, got excited, spent six weeks building, shipped something genuinely clever. Response? "Cool project." Zero paying users. The idea was mine, the validation was imaginary.

Project 2: A prospect mentioned a pain point on a sales call. I built a quick version over a weekend. Got a few users, broke even on costs, but the pain wasn't sharp enough for people to switch from their current workflow.

Project 3: Three separate prospects described the same problem in almost identical language within the same week. I built exactly what they described. Didn't try to make it elegant. Just solved the stated problem. That one has paying users and growing word of mouth.

The pattern: the further the idea originated from my own head, the better it performed. My technical taste was irrelevant. The market's stated need was the only reliable signal.

I'm not against building for yourself. But I've learned to separate "problems I find interesting" from "problems people will pay to solve." The overlap is smaller than most founders think.

One flop, one break-even, one win. Same founder, same year, same amount of effort. The only variable was where the idea came from.

The flop was a technically interesting project that solved a problem I personally had. I assumed others had it too. They didn't. Or at least not enough to change their behavior. I learned this after building for six weeks, not before.

The break-even was smarter. I validated that a pain point existed before building. But the validation was shallow. People said "yeah, that's annoying" in interviews. What I didn't validate was whether the pain was bad enough to make them switch from their existing workaround.

The win was almost accidental. Three different prospects described the exact same problem unprompted during sales calls. Same words. Same frustration. I built a focused solution in two weeks. They started paying before I had documentation.

The lesson isn't "always validate." Everyone says that. The lesson is: there's a hierarchy of demand signals. "I find this interesting" is the weakest. "People agree this is a problem" is better. "People are actively describing this pain without prompting" is the one that predicts revenue.

I now have a rule: I don't build anything unless I've heard the same pain from three unrelated sources.

posts.title: AI agents cant finish real tasks yet
posts.hook: I gave 4 different AI agent setups the same task last week: research 50 companies, enrich contacts, score them, draft outreach. Completion rate across all four: 0%.
posts.body:
I gave 4 different AI agent setups the same task last week: research 50 companies, enrich contacts, score them, draft outreach. Completion rate across all four: 0%.

Not because the models are bad. Because real-world tasks have branching failure modes that agents can't navigate yet without guardrails.

Company 12 had no LinkedIn page. Agent stalled. Company 23 returned a 403 from the enrichment API. Agent retried infinitely. Company 37 had two people with the same title. Agent picked randomly instead of flagging ambiguity.

The agents that "work" in production aren't autonomous. They're supervised pipelines with human-designed error handling at every junction.

My production outbound pipeline has 14 explicit error handlers. API timeout? Fall back to cache. No LinkedIn match? Skip and flag for manual review. Ambiguous title match? Queue for human decision. Enrichment confidence below threshold? Don't send, add to nurture.

That's not an agent doing a task. That's a human designing every failure path and letting an agent execute the happy path.

We'll get to real agent autonomy eventually. But right now, the value is in building the error handling, not in trusting the model to figure it out.

remixes.label: guardrail-taxonomy
remixes.hook: AI agents don't fail because the model is bad. They fail because nobody mapped the failure modes before hitting 'run'.
remixes.body:
AI agents don't fail because the model is bad. They fail because nobody mapped the failure modes before hitting 'run'.

I tested four different agent setups on a real GTM task: research 50 companies, enrich contacts, score leads, draft outreach. None of them completed it. Not one.

But the failures were instructive. They fell into exactly three categories.

Category 1: Data availability failures. Company 12 had no LinkedIn page. Company 31 was acquired and the domain redirected. The agent treated missing data like an error instead of an expected condition.

Category 2: API boundary failures. 403 errors, rate limits, schema changes, timeouts. The agent had no fallback path when an external service didn't cooperate.

Category 3: Judgment failures. Company 28 was a perfect ICP fit but the agent scored it low because the website copy didn't match the scoring rubric literally. The agent couldn't apply nuance.

Here's what actually works: you build a guardrail layer for each category. Default values and skip logic for missing data. Retry with backoff plus alternative sources for API failures. Human-in-the-loop checkpoints for judgment calls.

The agent doesn't need to be autonomous. It needs to know when to ask for help and what to do when things break.

remixes.hook: "Fully autonomous AI agents" is a marketing phrase, not a production architecture. Here's what agent pipelines actually look like when money is on the line.
remixes.body:
"Fully autonomous AI agents" is a marketing phrase, not a production architecture. Here's what agent pipelines actually look like when money is on the line.

I run a GTM pipeline that uses AI agents for research, enrichment, scoring, and outreach drafting. On paper, it's automated end to end. In reality, it has nine human checkpoints.

Checkpoint 1: After research, I review the company list for obvious mismatches. The agent sometimes confuses similarly named companies.

Checkpoint 2: After enrichment, I verify contact accuracy. Wrong titles, outdated roles, and merged companies create garbage downstream.

Checkpoint 3: After scoring, I eyeball the top and bottom 10%. The scoring model has blind spots I know about but haven't fixed yet.

Checkpoints 4 through 9: Various quality gates on the outreach itself. Tone, accuracy, personalization depth, compliance.

Is this slower than fully autonomous? Yes. Does it actually produce results I can send to real humans? Also yes.

The teams getting value from AI agents right now aren't the ones with the most sophisticated models. They're the ones who figured out where the human checkpoints need to be. They treat agents like junior analysts, not autonomous operators. Let them do the heavy lifting, verify the output, course-correct where needed.

Full autonomy is a goal, not a starting point.

posts.title: career pivot is a systems migration
posts.hook: Plumber to GTM engineer to founder. People ask how. The honest answer: I treated it like a systems migration, not a career pivot.
posts.body:
Plumber to GTM engineer to founder. People ask how. The honest answer: I treated it like a systems migration, not a career pivot.

In plumbing, you learn a framework: diagnose the problem, trace it to the root cause, fix it at the source, test the system, move on. You don't patch leaks with tape. You replace the section of pipe.

That's exactly how I approach GTM systems now. Company has low reply rates? I don't test new subject lines. I trace it back. Is the list right? Is the enrichment accurate? Is the timing aligned with intent? Is the channel correct? Fix the root cause.

The technical skills transferred more than I expected. Reading system diagrams, understanding flow and pressure, debugging by working backwards from the symptom. Swap "water pressure" for "pipeline velocity" and the mental model is the same.

What actually changed: the tools. Coding agents closed the gap between "I know exactly what this system should do" and "I can make a computer do it." That gap used to require a CS degree or a $150k hire. Now it requires Claude Code and persistence.

The career pivot narrative sounds dramatic. The reality was incremental. Same problem-solving framework, different domain, better tools.

If you're making a similar jump, stop thinking about the skills you lack. Map the skills you already have onto the new domain. You'll be surprised how much transfers.

The best debugging framework I've ever used isn't from a computer science textbook. It's from plumbing.

In plumbing, when a system fails, you don't start by guessing. You trace the flow. Water comes in here, moves through these pipes, exits there. You find where the expected flow diverges from reality. That's your problem.

I use the exact same approach on broken GTM systems. Leads come in here, get enriched through these steps, route through these conditions, convert there. When conversion drops, I trace the flow and find where reality diverges from the design.

Last month a client's pipeline was generating plenty of leads but zero meetings. The team was tweaking email copy. I traced the flow. The leads were entering the sequence with wrong persona tags because the enrichment step was using outdated job title mappings. No amount of copy optimization fixes bad routing.

Trades teach you systems thinking in a way that's physical and immediate. You can see when water flows wrong. You can feel when pressure drops. That visceral understanding of how systems behave translates directly to diagnosing any complex system, whether it carries water or data.

The non-obvious advantage of a trades background isn't grit or work ethic, though those help. It's the instinct to trace problems to their root instead of patching symptoms.

remixes.hook: When I tell people I went from plumber to GTM engineer to founder, they hear an inspirational story. What actually happened was a cold, methodical process of replacing one system with another.
remixes.body:
When I tell people I went from plumber to GTM engineer to founder, they hear an inspirational story. What actually happened was a cold, methodical process of replacing one system with another.

Phase 1: I mapped the skills I had against the skills the new field required. Plumbing gave me diagnostics, systems thinking, client communication, and project scoping. I was missing technical implementation, marketing knowledge, and industry vocabulary.

Phase 2: I filled the gaps with the minimum viable effort. Not a degree. Not a bootcamp. I took on one small GTM project for free, learned what I needed to deliver it, and used that project as proof of capability for the next one.

Phase 3: I iterated. Each project taught me what I was still missing. I filled those gaps for the next project. Within 18 months I had a portfolio of work that spoke louder than any credential.

Phase 4: I noticed that every company I worked with had the same structural problems. That's when the founder idea emerged. Not from ambition. From pattern recognition across enough projects.
